extractor.note: source_sha256 is the LF digest (CRLF checkout; local validate reports a false staleness, CI on LF passes). This commentary covers only Ideas I §§111-153 (the close of the third section and the fourth section, Reason and Reality); these are technical noetic-noematic analyses with sparse historical reference. The explicit predecessor engagement is with Kant (the 'Idea in the Kantian sense', §143), Descartes (the demon fiction as a skeptical worry, §145), and Twardowski (the act/content/object distinction, §129). One record per commentary covering all predecessors.

coverage_note: Covers the thin explicit predecessor engagement of Ideas I §§111-153: Kant (the perfect givenness of a thing, unreachable in any finite appearance, designated an 'Idea in the Kantian sense' — an absolutely determinate system of endless continuous appearing that lies insightfully before us as the idea of an essentially motivated infinity), Descartes (the Cartesian demon fiction as a skeptical worry that the index- and feeling-theories of evidence cannot overcome), and Twardowski (the distinction of act, content, and object, praised as a great advance since his treatise, whose radical development required a systematic phenomenology of consciousness). Not covered: the earlier parts of Ideas I on the natural attitude, the reduction, and noesis-noema in general, which lie outside this commentary's section range.

engagements.claim: Since a thing cannot be given in a closed, completed appearance, Husserl designates its perfect givenness as an 'Idea' in the Kantian sense: an absolutely determinate system of endless continuous appearing, prefigured and lying insightfully before us as the idea of an essentially motivated infinity.
engagements.quote: as an "Idea" (in the Kantian sense), perfect givenness is nonetheless **prefigured**—as an absolutely determinate system of endless processes of continuous appearing

engagements.claim: Husserl rejects the index- and feeling-theories of evidence, which treat evidence as a mystical voice from a better world, together with the skeptical worries such as the Cartesian demon fiction that those theories cannot overcome.
engagements.quote: Husserl rejects the index- and feeling-theories of evidence, as well as the skeptical worries (the Cartesian demon fiction) they cannot overcome.

predecessor.author: Kasimir Twardowski
predecessor.text: Zur Lehre vom Inhalt und Gegenstand der Vorstellungen

engagements.claim: Husserl acknowledges Twardowski's merit in the distinction of act, content, and object, praised as a great advance since his treatise, while holding that a radical advance was impossible before a systematic phenomenology of consciousness.
engagements.quote: Husserl reflects on the recent habit of praising the distinction between act, content, and object as a great advance (especially since Twardowski's treatise). While acknowledging Twardowski's merit, he notes that a radical advance was impossible before a systematic phenomenology of consciousness.
